source_text: Ὑπείδετο δὲ ὁ Κέλσος τὸ ἀπὸ τῆς γραφῆς ποιήσας τὸν Ἰησοῦν εἰρηκέναι ὅτι σατανᾶς τις τοιαῦτα παραμηχανήσεται. ἀλλὰ καὶ συναρπάζει τὸν λόγον φάσκων μὴ ἔξαρνον εἶναι τὸν Ἰησοῦν, ὡς ταῦτα οὐδὲν θεῖον ἔχει ἀλλὰ πονηρῶν ἐστιν ἔργα· ὁμογενῆ γὰρ αὐτὰ πεποίηκεν ἑτερογενῆ τυγχάνοντα. καὶ ὥσπερ λύκος κυνὶ οὐχ ὁμογενὴς, κἂν δοκῇ ἔχειν τι παραπλήσιον ἐν τῷ τοῦ σώματος σχήματι καὶ τῇ φωνῇ, οὐδὲ φάσσα τῇ περιστερᾷ· οὕτως οὐδὲν ὅμοιον ἔχει τὸ δυνάμει θεοῦ ἐπιτελούμενον τῷ γινομένῳ ἀπὸ γοητείας. ἔτι δὲ καὶ ταῦτα πρὸς τὰς Κέλσου κακουργίας ἐροῦμεν· ἆρα δυνάμεις γίνονται μὲν κατὰ γοητείαν ἀπὸ πονηρῶν δαιμόνων, οὐδεμία δὲ δύναμις ἐπιτελεῖται ἀπὸ τῆς θείας καὶ μακαρίας φύσεως, ἀλλ᾿ ὁ βίος τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἤνεγκε μὲν τὰ χείρονα οὐδαμῶς δ᾿ ἐχώρησε τὰ κρείττονα; καὶ τοῦτο δὲ δοκεῖ μοι ὥσπερ ἐπὶ πάντων δεῖν παρατιθέναι, ὅτι ὅπου τι χεῖρον προσποιούμενον εἶναι ὁμογενὲς τῷ κρείττονι, ἐκεῖ πάντως ἐκ τοῦ ἐναντίου ἐστί τι κρεῖττον. οὕτω καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν κατὰ γοητείαν ἐπιτελούντων. ὅτι πάντως ἀνάγκη εἶναι καὶ ἀπὸ θείας ἐνεργείας ἐν τῷ βίῳ γινόμενα. καὶ τοῦ αὐτοῦ ἐστιν ἐξ ἀκολουθίας ἤτοι ἀμφότερα ἀναιρεῖν καὶ λέγειν μηδέτερον γίνεσθαι ἢ τιθέντα τὸ ἕτερον καὶ μάλιστα τὸ χεῖρον ὁμολογεῖν καὶ περὶ τοῦ κρείττονος. εἰ δέ τις τιθείη μὲν τὰ ἀπὸ γοητείας γίνεσθαι, μὴ τιθείη δὲ τὰ ἀπὸ θείας δυνάμεως, δοκεῖ μοι παραπλήσιος εἶναι τῷ τιθέναι μὲν ὅτι εἰσὶ σοφίσματα καὶ λόγοι πιθανοὶ, ἀποτυγχάνοντες τῆς ἀληθείας, προσποιούμενοι τἀληθῆ παριστάνειν, οὐδαμοῦ δὲ παρ᾿ ἀνθρώποις ἀλήθεια καὶ διαλεκτικὴ ἀλλοτρία σοφισμάτων πολιτεύεται. εἰ δ᾿ ἅπαξ παραδεξόμεθα ἀκόλουθον εἶναι τῷ ὑποστατὴν εἶναι μαγείαν καὶ γοητείαν, ἐνεργουμένην ὑπὸ πονηρῶν δαιμόνων, κατακλήσεσι περιέργοις θελγομένων καὶ ἀνθρώποις γόησιν ὑπακουόντων, τὸ καὶ ἀπὸ θείας δυνάμεως δεῖν εὑρίσκεσθαι ἐν ἀνθρώποις· διὰ τί οὐχὶ καὶ βεβασανισμένως τοὺς ἐπαγ γελλομένους τὰς δυνάμεις ἐξετάσομεν ἀπὸ τοῦ βίου καὶ τοῦ ἤθους καὶ τῶν ἐπακολουθούντων ταῖς δυνάμεσιν ἤτοι εἰς βλάβην τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἢ εἰς ἠθῶν ἐπανόρθωσιν, τίς μὲν δαίμοσι διακονούμενος διά τινων ἐπῳδῶν καὶ μαγγανειῶν τὰ τοιαῦτα ποιεῖ, τίς δ᾿ ἐν χώρᾳ καθαρᾷ καὶ ἁγίᾳ γενόμενος κατὰ τὴν ψυχὴν ἑαυτοῦ καὶ τὸ πνεῦμα, οἶμαι δὲ καὶ τὸ σῶμα, τῷ θεῷ, παραδεξάμενος θεῖόν τι πνεῦμα τὰ τοιαῦτα εἰς ὠφέλειαν ἀνθρώπων καὶ προτροπὴν τὴν ἐπὶ τὸ πιστεύειν θεῷ ἀληθινῷ πράττει; εἰ δ᾿ ἅπαξ ζητεῖν δεῖ μὴ συναρπαζόμενον ὑπὸ τῶν δυνάμεων, τίς μὲν ἀπὸ κρείττονος τίς δὲ ἀπὸ χείρονος τὰ τοιαῦτα ἐπιτελεῖ, ἵνα ἢ μὴ πάντα κακολογῶμεν ἢ μὴ πάντα ὡς θεῖα θαυμάζωμεν καὶ ἀποδεχώμεθα· πῶς οὐχὶ προφανὲς μὲν ἔσται ἐκ τῶν συμβάντων ἐπὶ Μωϋσέως καὶ ἐπὶ Ἰησοῦ, ἐθνῶν ὅλων συστάντων μετὰ τὰ σημεῖα αὐτῶν, ὅτι θείᾳ δυνάμει πεποιήκασιν οὗτοι ἅπερ ἀναγέγραπται αὐτοὺς πεποιηκέναι; οὐκ ἂν γὰρ πονηρία καὶ μαγγανεία ὅλον ἔθνος συνέστησαν, ὑπερβὰν μὲν οὐ μόνον ἀγάλματα καὶ τὰ ὑπ᾿ ἀνθρώπων ἱδρυμένα ἀλλὰ καὶ πᾶσαν γενητὴν φύσιν. ἀναβαῖνον δὲ πρὸς τὴν ἀγένητον τοῦ θεοῦ τῶν ὅλων ἀρχήν.
pass_a_gloss: Celsus surmised (ὑφοράομαι, aor. mid. ὑπείδετο) [it], having from Scripture (γραφή) made Jesus to have said that a certain Satan will contrive such things. But he also seizes/rushes (συναρπάζω) the argument, claiming (φάσκω) Jesus is not denying (ἔξαρνος) that these have nothing divine but are works of wicked men; for he made them of one kind (ὁμογενής) though they are of different kinds (ἑτερογενής). And as a wolf (λύκος) is not of one kind with a dog (κύων), even if it seems to have something similar in the shape (σχῆμα) of the body and the voice (φωνή), nor the wood pigeon (φάσσα) with the dove (περιστερά), so nothing similar has the thing accomplished by power of God to what comes about from sorcery. Further we will say these things also against Celsus's malpractices (κακουργίαι): do powers come about by sorcery from evil demons (πονηροὶ δαίμονες), but no power is accomplished from the divine and blessed nature (θεία καὶ μακαρία φύσις), but the life of men bore (φέρω) the worse (χείρονα) but in no way made room for (χωρέω) the better (κρείττονα)? And this seems to me to need to be set beside (παρατίθημι) as in all cases: that where something worse pretends (προσποιέομαι) to be of one kind with the better, there wholly from the opposite (ἐναντίον) there is something better. So also in the case of those accomplishing by sorcery: that wholly there must be also things coming about in life from divine working (θεία ἐνέργεια). And it belongs to the same [person] by consequence (ἀκολουθία) either to abolish (ἀναιρέω) both and say neither comes about, or, positing (τίθημι) the one and especially the worse, to confess also about the better. And if someone should posit the things from sorcery to come about, but not posit those from divine power, he seems to me similar to positing that there are sophisms (σοφίσματα) and persuasive (πιθανός) arguments, missing (ἀποτυγχάνω) the truth, pretending to present (παριστάνω) the truths, but nowhere among men does truth and dialectic (διαλεκτική) foreign to sophisms live as citizen (πολιτεύομαι). And if once we accept it to be consequent (ἀκόλουθον) on magic (μαγεία) and sorcery being real/subsistent (ὑποστατός), worked by evil demons charmed (θέλγω) by curious/magical invocations (κατακλήσεσι περιέργοις) and obeying (ὑπακούω) sorcerer men, that [what is] from divine power must be found among men, why shall we not also examine (ἐξετάζω) testingly (βεβασανισμένως) those professing the powers, from their life (βίος) and character (ἦθος) and the things following (ἐπακολουθέω) the powers, either to harm (βλάβη) of men or to correction (ἐπανόρθωσις) of morals (ἤθη): who, serving (διακονέω) demons, through certain incantations (ἐπῳδαί) and trickeries (μαγγανεῖαι) does such things, and who, having come into a pure and holy place/standing (χώρα καθαρὰ καὶ ἁγία) as to his soul (ψυχή) and spirit (πνεῦμα), and I think also body (σῶμα), to God, having received some divine spirit (θεῖόν τι πνεῦμα) does such things for benefit (ὠφέλεια) of men and exhortation (προτροπή) to believe in the true God (θεὸς ἀληθινός)? And if once one must seek, not being carried away (συναρπάζομαι) by the powers, who from the better and who from the worse accomplishes such things, so that we neither speak ill (κακολογέω) of all nor admire (θαυμάζω) and accept (ἀποδέχομαι) all as divine, how will it not be manifest (προφανής) from the things that happened under Moses and under Jesus, whole nations (ἔθνη) having been constituted (συνίστημι) after their signs, that by divine power these did what is recorded of them? For wickedness (πονηρία) and trickery (μαγγανεία) would not have constituted a whole nation, passing beyond (ὑπερβαίνω) not only statues (ἀγάλματα) and the things set up (ἱδρύω) by men but also all generated nature (γενητὴ φύσις), and ascending (ἀναβαίνω) to the ungenerated (ἀγένητος) first principle (ἀρχή) of the God of all (θεὸς τῶν ὅλων).
pass_b_english: Celsus caught a hint from Scripture when he made Jesus say that “a certain Satan” will contrive such things. But he also snatches at a conclusion when he claims that Jesus does not deny “that these works have nothing divine about them but are the deeds of wicked men”; for he has made them of one kind when they are in fact of different kinds. As a wolf is not of one kind with a dog, even if it seems to have some likeness in the shape of its body and in its voice, nor the wood pigeon with the dove, so what is accomplished by the power of God is nothing like what comes from sorcery.

We will say this as well against Celsus’s malicious arguments. Are mighty works done by sorcery through evil demons, while no mighty work at all is accomplished by the divine and blessed nature? Has human life borne the worse things, yet had no room at all for the better? It seems to me that this principle should be laid down as applying in every case: wherever something worse pretends to be of one kind with the better, there is certainly something better on the other side. So too with those who work by sorcery: there must certainly also be things that happen in this life through divine working. And by the same logic one must either do away with both and say that neither happens, or, if one grants the one, and especially the worse, admit the better as well. But if someone were to grant that things happen through sorcery yet not grant those that come through divine power, he seems to me like a man who grants that there are sophisms and plausible arguments which fall short of the truth while pretending to present it, but holds that truth, and a dialectic free of sophistry, has its home nowhere among men.

But if once we accept that, given the real existence of magic and sorcery worked by evil demons, who are charmed by magical invocations and obey sorcerers, it follows that what comes from divine power must also be found among men, why should we not also examine rigorously those who claim these powers, judging by their life, by their character, and by what follows from their powers, whether harm to people or the reform of their morals, to see who does such things in the service of demons through certain incantations and tricks, and who, having come into a pure and holy standing before God in his soul and spirit, and I think also in his body, and having received some divine spirit, does such things for people’s benefit and to urge them to believe in the true God. And if once we must inquire, without being carried away by the powers, who accomplishes such things from the better source and who from the worse, so that we neither revile them all nor admire and accept them all as divine, how will it not be plain from what took place under Moses and under Jesus, when whole nations were formed after their signs, that these men did by divine power the things that they are recorded to have done? For wickedness and trickery would not have formed a whole nation that rose above not only statues and the things set up by men, but also every created nature, and ascended to the uncreated first principle, the God of all.

choices.why: ὑπείδετο: 'was guessing from Scripture' -> 'caught a hint from Scripture'
οὐδὲν ὅμοιον ἔχει: 'has nothing in common with' -> 'is nothing like'
one Greek question kept as one: removed added 'We may judge' sentence; βεβασανισμένως -> 'rigorously'; ἐπαγγελλομένους τὰς δυνάμεις -> 'claim these powers'

2.51 opening: ὑπείδετο with τὸ ἀπὸ τῆς γραφῆς is a hard construction; rendered 'Celsus caught a hint from Scripture', with a note. Passed, but worth a look from the owner if a second reading is wanted.
2.51 close: τὴν ἀγένητον τοῦ θεοῦ τῶν ὅλων ἀρχήν kept as an appositive ('the uncreated first principle, the God of all'), as the translator's note explains.

translator_notes: ὑπείδετο (ὑφοράομαι, ‘suspect, surmise’): Origen’s point is that Celsus took ‘a certain Satan’ from a guess at Scripture (the ‘working of Satan’ of 2 Thessalonians 2:9, quoted in 2.50), since Jesus’ own words in 2.49 do not name Satan; rendered ‘was guessing from Scripture’. The short phrases quoted in the first paragraph repeat Celsus’s words from 2.49 and are put in quotation marks. συναρπάζει τὸν λόγον: ‘snatches at a conclusion’ (seizes the argument unfairly). φάσσα / περιστερά: wood pigeon (ring-dove) and domestic dove. κατακλήσεσι περιέργοις: περίεργος is the usual word for magical arts (as in Acts 19:19), hence ‘magical invocations’; no citation, since not an allusion. ἐν χώρᾳ καθαρᾷ καὶ ἁγίᾳ γενόμενος ... τῷ θεῷ: rendered ‘having come into a pure and holy standing before God’. The neuter participles ὑπερβάν and ἀναβαῖνον agree with ἔθνος. γενητός / ἀγένητος are rendered ‘created’ / ‘uncreated’; τὴν ἀγένητον τοῦ θεοῦ τῶν ὅλων ἀρχήν is taken as ‘the uncreated first principle, the God of all’ (an appositive genitive). No Scripture is quoted in this chapter; the signs of Moses and Jesus are general references already cited in 2.48-2.50. Reviewer: ὑπείδετο with τὸ ἀπὸ τῆς γραφῆς is difficult; ‘caught a hint from Scripture’ keeps Origen’s point that the Satan detail came from Scripture (2 Thessalonians 2:9), not from Jesus’ words. The appositive reading of τὴν ἀγένητον τοῦ θεοῦ τῶν ὅλων ἀρχήν is kept.
